questions.question_stem: A team says its service is not really distributed because users see one coherent application rather than many machines. Which response best matches the lesson's definition?
questions.correct_answer: It can still be distributed if multiple networked nodes cooperate behind the scenes to appear as one service.
incorrect_answers: It cannot be deemed distributed if a frontend hides individual nodes behind one coherent service view.
It must be classified as centralized if the system uses web APIs to synchronize state across its nodes.
It is only considered distributed if it eliminates administrative roles and control structures entirely.
questions.explanation: The lesson defines a distributed system by the implementation: multiple networked nodes must coordinate despite independent failures and unreliable communication while presenting a coherent service to users.

questions.question_stem: A file-sharing system removes its central coordinator and lets peers discover and transfer data through an overlay. Which tradeoff is most consistent with the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: It reduces mandatory dependence on one hub but increases coordination, routing, and consistency challenges.
incorrect_answers: It guarantees full operational isolation among nodes but eliminates standard latency and routing issues.
It eliminates operational costs on each client but guarantees immediate, network-wide data replication.
It ensures precise request paths for transfers but increases single-point vulnerabilities for peer nodes.
questions.explanation: The lesson rejects the idea that decentralization is automatically better. P2P designs can improve resilience against single-point failure or takedown, but they add coordination cost, path complexity, and temporary disagreement.

questions.question_stem: In a Napster-like design, a central index helps users find files while the files transfer directly between peers. What lesson point does this architecture illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: Centralizing discovery can improve usability and search while creating a legal, policy, and technical chokepoint.
incorrect_answers: Sharing data transfer can remove bandwidth bottlenecks while forcing strict administrative parity among peers.
Decentralizing control can guarantee total security while avoiding transport costs for every participant.
Standardizing interfaces can avoid message loss and latency while ensuring uniform client software versions.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses Napster to show a hybrid split: centralized discovery with peer-to-peer transfer. That split makes search efficient and governable, but it concentrates control and failure risk in the index.

questions.question_stem: A Gnutella-style search network has no central index, so each query is forwarded to many neighbors with a TTL. Why can this scale poorly even though it avoids a single index server?
questions.correct_answer: Flooding creates redundant traffic and bandwidth pressure as queries spread across overlapping paths.
incorrect_answers: Flooding guarantees one clean route per query and prunes duplicates before any neighbor forwards them.
Flooding makes every peer maintain a central index, so searches fail whenever that index server goes down.
Flooding reduces bandwidth use by sending each query only to one closest peer that stores the requested file.
questions.explanation: The lesson presents naive flooding as a controlled but costly replacement for centralized lookup. Duplicate forwarding, overlapping paths, and relay burden can become the new bottleneck.

questions.question_stem: A checkout service keeps running, but one payment dependency is slow, one region is unreachable, and cached product pages still load. What concept best describes this situation?
questions.correct_answer: Partial failure, because some components or paths fail while other parts of the system continue operating.
incorrect_answers: Total failure, because any single slow dependency forces every node and cache to halt immediately together.
Homogeneous failure, because all servers must crash with the same software error before users notice issues.
Consensus failure, because a payment timeout means every region has already accepted conflicting ledger state.
questions.explanation: Distributed systems often fail in pieces: nodes, dependencies, paths, racks, zones, or services can break independently. Mitigations include isolation, timeouts, retries, replication, and graceful degradation.

questions.question_stem: Two designs have the same rate of failures, but one restores service much faster after each incident. Which availability claim follows from the lesson's MTTF and MTTR framing?
questions.correct_answer: The faster-recovering design can provide better availability by reducing MTTR even if MTTF is unchanged.
incorrect_answers: The highly resilient design can guarantee perfect availability by ignoring MTTR once MTTF is estimated later.
The faster recovering design improves reliability by increasing MTTR while keeping failure frequency fixed.
The redundant design makes availability independent of recovery time because MTTF fully replaces MTTR metrics.
questions.explanation: The lesson ties availability to both how often failures occur and how quickly the system recovers. Increasing MTTF and reducing MTTR are both reliability levers.

questions.question_stem: A client submits a transfer request, times out, and cannot tell whether the server processed the transfer before the response was lost. Which design response best addresses this ambiguity?
questions.correct_answer: Use request identifiers and idempotent retry handling so repeating the request does not duplicate the side effect.
incorrect_answers: Use transaction sequencing and synchronous message confirmation so executing the process does not require a timeout.
Use automatic network rerouting and topology discovery so losing a connection does not disrupt the application.
Use message hashing algorithms and public signatures so intercepting the packet won't compromise identities.
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that timeouts leave the outcome unknown. Idempotency and request IDs let systems retry safely when a response may have been lost after successful processing.

questions.question_stem: A student claims that because blockchain transactions are signed, a node does not need to worry about malicious peers or distorted network views. What is the best correction?
questions.correct_answer: Signatures authenticate data, but nodes still need peer diversity, validation, rate limits, and defenses against view manipulation.
incorrect_answers: Encryption secures transport, but networks still need routing protocols, full data redundancy, error checks, and static IP addresses.
Firewalls filter traffic, but managers still need manual auditing, version checks, license renewals, and physical server locks.
Passwords restrict access, but interfaces still need protocol standards, feature negotiations, schema rules, and translations.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates cryptographic authenticity from network security. Signed data can still arrive through malicious, unreliable, or strategically selected peers.

questions.question_stem: A blockchain node hears about a new transaction several seconds before some peers and after others. What does this show about gossip propagation?
questions.correct_answer: Gossip is probabilistic peer relay, so latency, bandwidth, and topology can give nodes temporarily different views.
incorrect_answers: Routing is deterministic path selection, so encryption, message size, and security can give nodes identical pathways.
Flooding is swift global broadcast, so bandwidth, packet loss, and topology can give nodes stable ledgers.
Validation is centralized query, so latency, hardware drift, and churn can give nodes unified histories.
questions.explanation: The lesson links blockchain gossip to controlled flooding rather than omniscient broadcast. Nodes validate and relay through changing peer paths, so temporary disagreement is expected.

questions.question_stem: Why do supernodes in Gnutella-like overlays and full nodes in blockchain networks illustrate a similar distributed-systems pattern?
questions.correct_answer: Both introduce a partial hierarchy where stronger, more available nodes reduce overhead or provide validation and data service for weaker clients.
incorrect_answers: Both establish a strict centralization where single, highly privileged servers mandate network routing or enforce access controls for ordinary nodes.
Both demand a complete homogenization where identical standard software packages eliminate latency or perform transaction signing for client nodes.
Both maintain a fixed configuration where constant reliable transport lines avoid congestion or deliver bandwidth capacity for wireless links.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses supernodes, leaves, full nodes, and light clients to show that overlays often evolve roles. Partial hierarchy can improve scalability while creating dependence on stronger peers.

questions.question_stem: A service performs hundreds of tiny remote calls because local tests made the network feel invisible. Which reading takeaway explains why this design may fail in production?
questions.correct_answer: Latency is not zero; many fine-grained remote calls multiply round-trip delay even when bandwidth is high.
incorrect_answers: Bandwidth is not finite; many parallel processing paths eliminate network bottlenecks even when latency is high.
Topology is static; fixed network routes ensure constant transmission speeds even when churn is high.
Security is simple; many cryptographic keys prevent peer identity theft even when network threats are high.
questions.explanation: The reading warns against treating networked computation like local computation. Hiding remoteness can encourage chatty APIs whose accumulated round trips hurt responsiveness over WANs or the Internet.

questions.question_stem: A designer tries to fix latency by batching every request into very large payloads, then finds that packet loss, relay cost, and low-bandwidth participants become major problems. What reading-based conclusion is best?
questions.correct_answer: Reducing round trips must be balanced against finite bandwidth, transport cost, and message-size limits.
incorrect_answers: Standardizing interfaces must be optimized against proprietary systems, platform types, and hardware limits.
Securing communications must be weighed against latency, decryption cost, and computing power budgets.
Caching remote data must be balanced against stale data, inconsistencies, and server storage limits.
questions.explanation: The reading pairs the latency and bandwidth fallacies: fewer, larger calls can reduce round trips, but unbounded payloads create congestion, cost, and participation pressure.

questions.question_stem: A public network upgrade assumes every operator will deploy the same software version on the same day, with identical monitoring and permissions. Which reading insight most directly challenges this plan?
questions.correct_answer: Distributed systems cross administrative and heterogeneous environments, so upgrades need compatibility, diagnostics, and staged coordination.
incorrect_answers: Decentralized overlays assume static homogeneous structures, so protocols need hardware standards, static IPs, and manual operator verification.
Adversarial networks avoid secure encrypted paths, so transactions need instant execution, global consensus, and cryptographic signatures.
Client-server systems manage unified local architectures, so databases need synchronous replication, instant queries, and zero-latency links.
questions.explanation: The reading emphasizes multiple administrators and heterogeneity as normal conditions. Independent policies, privileges, monitoring, versions, and implementations require public contracts, compatibility, and fallback planning.
